topics.topic: How startup handles failure to remove an unreferenced blob
questions: What happens when startup cannot remove an unreferenced value or fixture blob?
What happens when an unreferenced value-byte file cannot be removed: does startup fail, continue while ensuring the blob is never served, or continue and retry at a later start?
What happens when startup cannot remove unreferenced value bytes: does startup fail, continue while leaving them unreadable for a later cleanup, or take another action?

judgement.why: This is the same startup cleanup-failure question already decided in P1, and the deciding later-state passages have not changed.

precedent.topic: Required behavior when orphan value bytes cannot be verified or removed at startup
quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

run_start_sequence: [VALIDATION_ERROR] Every step is required: the first step that raises — InstallationRejectedError, RefusedError from the instance check, a store refusal, SandboxUnavailableError, StopRequiredError or any other exception — stops the sequence there and propagates unchanged to the caller with the step named in its reason; no later step runs and nothing is retried or skipped.
precedent.why: The later contracts require open_store to stop on its first failure and require any exception from that startup step to stop the entire start sequence.

topics.topic: Whether failed-run spool retention is exempt from startup cleanup
questions: Is a failed run's retained spool an exception to this new claim, or must startup remove it despite K-10 and A14?
Is this claim limited to the content-addressed value/fixture area, or does it override K-10 and A14, which require a failed run's spool files to outlive the run until release?

quotes:
On start, temporary files,
   value bytes no record names (left by a failed call, so only trial fixtures
   and named values outlive a run, K-10; owner, 2026-10-07) and
   the spool directories of runs that ended and do not keep their spool (A14) are
   removed; nothing else is.

A `failed` run keeps its spool until the owner or an agent releases it; release
removes the files, records who and when, and is refused for a run that is not
`failed` or was already released (K-10).
judgement.why: The first passage says only trial fixtures and named values outlive a run, while the second requires an ended failed run's spool to remain until release.

topics.topic: Whether startup cleanup includes unreferenced file-fixture blobs
questions: Must startup remove every unreferenced blob in the content-addressed value-and-fixture area, or only blobs for value-carriage StoredValues?

Does “value bytes” include an unreferenced file-fixture blob published by a failed trial-case or capture call, or must such a fixture remain because rule 2 distinguishes “value bytes and file fixtures” and rule 4 says nothing else is removed?

judgement.why: This is the same question about unreferenced trial-fixture cleanup already decided in P3, and the deciding later-state passage has not changed.

precedent.topic: Whether startup orphan cleanup includes unreferenced trial-fixture files
quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
precedent.why: The later startup note explicitly removes content-addressed files whose digest is named by neither a StoredValue nor a file-fixture record.

topics.topic: Which durable references make value bytes named and therefore preserved at startup
questions: Exactly which database references make a blob “named”: existence of its StoredValue record, a reference to that StoredValue from another durable record, any record containing its digest, or reachability from a specified set of root records?
When previously orphaned value bytes are reused by a successful call and become named before the next start, does startup preserve them or remove them?

quotes: open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on a lock file inside data_directory, opened without following links and held for the life of the process; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue and no file fixture record names, and create the database schema, the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.

Adds content-addressed bytes; writes no record. Bytes whose record never
follows — a later failure of the caller's attempt — stay unnamed; equal bytes
reuse them, and the next start removes them (A13 rule 3, A18 rule 4).
judgement.why: The later store contract defines naming by a StoredValue or file-fixture record, so reused bytes are preserved when the successful call creates such a record before startup cleanup.
